title: Air-dry clay mosaic picture frame
subtitle: A wide-bordered frame decorated with pressed clay tile pieces in a mosaic pattern
excerpt: This picture frame is built from a slab base with small clay tile pieces pressed into the border before drying to create a mosaic effect. The tiles can be stamped, embossed, or plain, and arranged in geometric or random patterns. No kiln required. The finished frame holds a 10 × 15 cm photograph.
sourceNotes: Slab and tile technique derived from first principles. Mosaic frame form documented in twentieth-century domestic craft publications; technique references derived from traditional slab-building and tile-making methodology.

glossaryTerms.definition: A flat sheet of clay rolled to even thickness, usually between two wooden guide rails.
Clay dissolved in water to a thick paste, used as adhesive when joining clay pieces.
Clay that has dried to a firm, pliable state: stiff enough to hold its shape but still damp enough to join with slurry or accept surface decoration.

content.text: A mosaic picture frame made from air-dry clay works differently from ceramic tile mosaic: instead of grouting gaps between pre-cut tiles, the small clay pieces are pressed onto a fresh clay base before drying so the base clay grips them as it dries. The result is a unified clay surface with a tile-pattern texture rather than individual inlaid pieces. The frame is decorative; seal thoroughly before displaying in a humid room.
What you'll need

Around 500 g of air-dry clay. A card template for the frame: outer rectangle 20 × 25 cm; inner rectangle 10 × 15 cm (the photo window). A small knife or craft cutter for trimming the tile pieces. Acrylic paint for finishing and two coats of sealant.
Rolling the base frame
Roll a
slab
to 6 mm thickness. Place the outer template (20 × 25 cm) on the slab and cut around it. Then cut out the inner photo window (10 × 15 cm), leaving a 5 cm border all around.
From the remaining slab, cut small tile pieces: 1.5 × 1.5 cm squares, or similar small shapes. You need enough to cover the frame border. Aim for about 60 to 80 small pieces.
Optional: while the tile pieces are still fresh, stamp each one with a pottery stamp, a fork tine, or a button to give texture. Rotate through two or three different stamps for variety.
Allow the frame base to firm to
leather-hard
before pressing on the tile pieces. At this stage the clay holds its shape but is still damp enough to grip the tiles. If the base is too soft, the tiles can sink in and warp it.
Apply a thin layer of
slurry

to the underside of each tile piece and press it firmly onto the frame border. Arrange the tiles in rows, offset like a brick pattern, or in a random arrangement. Leave narrow gaps between tiles: 2 to 3 mm: so the slurry-filled grout lines show when painted.
When all tiles are placed, press each one firmly with a fingertip to ensure contact. Trim any tiles that overhang the edge of the frame with the fettling knife.

Add a hanging strip: roll a coil 10 mm thick and 6 cm long. Flatten it slightly and score the centre back of the frame top edge. Apply slurry and press the coil on as a hanging loop, bending the ends of the coil down to rest flat against the frame back. This loop goes through the wall hook.
Drying

Dry the frame flat on a smooth tile for 48 hours. Cover loosely with a plastic bag for the first 24 hours to slow the surface drying of the tile pieces: if the tiles dry faster than the base, they can pop off. After 48 hours, remove the bag and allow to air-dry for another day.
Finishing

Paint the frame with acrylic paint, working the colour into the gaps between tiles. Before the paint dries completely, wipe the raised tile surfaces with a dry cloth to create a two-tone effect: darker colour in the grout lines and gaps, lighter colour on the tile faces. Apply two coats of sealant over the dried paint. Glue the photograph behind the frame window with a small piece of card backing, and attach the frame to a wall through the hanging loop.
Variations
Use two colours of air-dry clay for the tile pieces: alternate white and terracotta tiles for a checkerboard effect before the piece is painted.
Press small shells, pebbles, or glass nuggets into the base clay alongside or instead of clay tiles.
Make a mirror frame by the same method: replace the card backing and photograph with a small adhesive mirror piece glued to the back.

rows.problem: Tile pieces fall off during or after drying
rows.cause: Insufficient slurry on contact surface; base too dry when tiles were applied
rows.fix: Apply slurry to the underside of every tile. Press firmly and hold for five seconds. Apply tiles when the base is leather-hard, not bone-dry.

rows.problem: Frame base cracks or warps during drying
rows.cause: Uneven slab thickness; tiles pulled the base as they dried and shrank
rows.fix: Roll slabs to even 6 mm thickness. Add the hanging loop after the frame base has dried to leather-hard to avoid distorting it.

rows.problem: Grout lines too large or irregular
rows.cause: Tiles cut to unequal sizes; gaps left too wide
rows.fix: Cut tiles to the same size using a small ruler and knife. Space with a consistent gap: use a thin piece of card as a spacer.
